articles.text: The League of Women Voters of California (LWV), in partnership with Drive Clean California, is hosting a one-hour informational Zoom event that will highlight the benefits of electric vehicle (EV) ownership and include the latest trends, costs, and considerations for those interested in moving to electric. The event will be held this Saturday, July 10, at 5 p.m., and repeated on Wednesday, July 14, at 6 p.m. Both will feature EV and e-bike experts and owners, who will discuss government incentives, solutions for residents who live in apartments and additional financial incentives for disadvantaged communities. The events will aim to debunk common EV myths and will serve as an opportunity for anyone to ask questions about EV ownership. California residents will receive priority placement for Drive Clean’s EV discount program. The next discount will be available in November. Drive Clean was developed by the California Air Resources Board as a resource for car buyers that are looking to find the cleanest and most efficient car that meets their driving needs. It was created to provide information, tools, and resources that help Californians learn about advanced vehicle technologies, and state-funded financial incentives to promote EV ownership. Drive Clean California is a collaborative campaign that builds upon the success of Drive Clean Bay Area with a mission to rapidly decrease carbon emissions. For those who drive or ride electric, the LWV and Drive Clean invites you to help host a Zoom “breakout room” following the main presentation, where attendees can hear your experiences and ask you questions. Contact info@cooltheearth.org to sign up as a Zoom “breakout room” host. To register for the July 10 or July 14 event, visit https://drivecleancalifornia.org/league-ofwomen-voters/. A similar event sponsored by the LWV and Drive Clean will be held in October. articles.text: This week, we of the Jewish tradition will begin reading from the book of Deuteronomy as part of our weekly reading from the Torah. Deuteronomy is essentially a review – a review of the history of the Israelites from the time they left Egypt to the time they were preparing to enter the Promised Land. It is a review of what God expects from them (and us) and what happens when they do or do not hearken to God’s commandments. These reminders of Israelite history and admonitions to follow God’s laws are found in the final orations given by Moses in the book of Deuteronomy. It is hoped that from going over what has happened and what is expected that the children of Israel will learn to lead better lives and to follow God’s commandments more closely. This past week, those of us living in Oakland and the surrounding area wondered what would happen after the verdict in the Mehserle trial. Would there be violence, would there be uncontrolled rioting, would the city burn. Some in the city had the hope that none of this would happen and that the city would remain peaceful and life could go on as normal. Some hoped that those disagreeing with the verdict would be able to share their concern, their anger, their disenchantment, but do so in a constructive instead of destructive way. In reviewing what had happened after the killing of Oscar Grant, when the city of Oakland suffered much violence, had we learned anything at all? I believe the answer to that question is a definite “yes.” Just as the children of Israel in looking over their history and their relationship with God learned from the past and prepared for the future, so did the leaders in Oakland. Just as the children of Israel understand what was expected of them, the leaders in Oakland realized their responsibility as leaders. The leaders of our city devised a way to let people express their feelings in a non-violent manner as the stage was open to all. It was open mike for all who wanted to be heard. articles.text: Oakland City Council extends parklet program through 2022 Gov. Gavin Newsom visited San Francisco’s Richmond District last month to announce that the state’s Department of Beverage Control will allow restaurants to sell cocktails to-go until the end of 2021. He also announced his interests in making outdoor dining permanent and more accessible state-wide. Both have allowed small businesses in the food and beverage industry to stay afloat during the pandemic, he said. “We don’t want to go back to normal. Normal was never good enough,” Gov. Newsom said. “We want to keep parklets going. It’s a good thing for our public health. We want to encourage people to continue to dine outside.” The governor added that he sent letters “to city and local governments statewide” encouraging city leaders to continue and expand allowances for outdoor dining. But the decision to keep, expand, or eliminate the use of parklets is ultimately up to each individual city. Oakland extends parklets through next Spring Oakland’s City Council voted on June 2 to introduce an ordinance that would extend the Flex Streets Initiative until March 31, 2022. The City of Oakland created the initiative in May 2020 for businesses, especially those in the food and beverage industry, that were unable to serve indoors due to the county health order. Through an application process it allowed for flexible uses of sidewalks, parking lanes, and streets. The city also waived all fees and streamlined permitting for business’ use of public rights-of-way. The adjusted permitting process allows for expedited approval for business use in private parking lots and outdoor areas, city-owned outdoor properties and traffic lanes. Businesses may use these spaces for extra seating, expanded merchandise displays, or customer queuing. To date, the city has approved more than 100 sidewalk cafes and parklets, 13 street closures, and more than 40 mobile vendors throughout the pandemic. In March, the City posted an interactive map of its Flex Streets program, which can be viewed by visiting https://oakgis.maps.arcgis.com/home/webmap/viewer. html?webmap=f8b30e3e36924ead83960173e556146f/. gov/FlexStreets. State legislation could make parklets permanent Senate Bill 314, proposed in the state legislature by Sen. Scott Wiener [D-San Francisco] and called the Bar and Restaurant Recovery Act, proposes several amendments to California’s liquor laws that intend to make them more flexible. If passed, some parklets would become permanent, also meaning restaurants would have the ability to serve alcohol on sidewalks and parking lots. “This expanded outdoor seating and service area – previously prohibited under California’s alcohol laws – has allowed restaurants and bars to survive and has been wildly popular with the public, with a more European-feeling street life,” said Wiener. The bill would also make it easier for bars and restaurants to share commercial, outdoor space with each other, and music venues would no longer need to have full kitchens in order to obtain a liquor license. SB 314 passed unanimously in committee in April, and enjoys bi-partisan support. It is co-authored by Sen. Andreas Borgeas (R-Fresno) and Sen. Jim Nielsen (R-Red Bluff). To learn more about Oakland flex streets program, call 510- 238-7398 or visit OaklandCA. Oakland City Council has agreed to extend its “Flex Streets” parklet program. articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Department recently announced the promotion of Katrina Morris to Recreation Supervisor on July 1. In her new position Morris will supervise the Department’s Preschool Programs and continue her work with the Schoolmates. Morris joined the Department as a Recreation Leader at Havens Schoolmates in 2004. Her creativity, natural leadership qualities, and love for kids helped her develop into a key staff member in the Schoolmates program. Morris continued to move her way up in the Department by becoming the Assistant Site Coordinator at Beach Schoolmates, Site Coordinator at Wildwood, and most recently as Schoolmates Childcare Program Coordinator. Morris also directed many of the Department’s summer camps, including Healthy Hoppers, Cre- 8tive Design, and Camp Everything. Last fall she was selected to represent the City of Piedmont in the Alameda County Leadership Academy. “I am excited to acquire new responsibilities and to continue Newly named Recreation Supervisor Katrina Morris. my work in the department. I fell in love with the importance of play and this community in 2004 and will continue to nurture and grow our childcare programs,” said Morris. “I am so thrilled Katrina is our newest Recreation Supervisor,” said Recreation Director Chelle Putzer. “She brings not only 17 years of experience to the position but a true passion and love of working with children.”

pages.text: Wednesday, July 7, 2021 3 Outdoor dining, to-go drinks could be permanent Oakland City Council extends parklet program through 2022 By Allyson Aleksey Gov. Gavin Newsom visited San Francisco’s Richmond District last month to announce that the state’s Department of Beverage Control will allow restaurants to sell cocktails to-go until the end of 2021. He also announced his interests in making outdoor dining permanent and more accessible state-wide. Both have allowed small businesses in the food and beverage industry to stay afloat during the pandemic, he said. “We don’t want to go back to normal. Normal was never good enough,” Gov. Newsom said. “We want to keep parklets going. It’s a good thing for our public health. We want to encourage people to continue to dine outside.” The governor added that he sent letters “to city and local governments statewide” encouraging city leaders to continue and expand allowances for outdoor dining. But the decision to keep, expand, or eliminate the use of parklets is ultimately up to each individual city. Oakland extends parklets through next Spring Oakland’s City Council voted on June 2 to introduce an ordinance that would extend the Flex Streets Initiative until March 31, 2022. The City of Oakland created the initiative in May 2020 for businesses, especially those in the food and beverage industry, that were unable to serve indoors due to the county health order. Through an application process it allowed for flexible uses of sidewalks, parking lanes, and streets. The city also waived all fees and streamlined permitting for business’ use of public rights-of-way. The adjusted permitting process allows for expedited approval for business use in private parking lots and outdoor areas, city-owned outdoor properties and traffic lanes. Businesses may use these spaces for extra seating, expanded merchandise displays, or customer queuing. To date, the city has approved more than 100 sidewalk cafes and parklets, 13 street closures, and more than 40 mobile vendors throughout the pandemic. In March, the City posted an interactive map of its Flex Streets program, which can be viewed by visiting https://oakgis.maps.arcgis.com/home/webmap/viewer. html?webmap=f8b30e3e36924ead83960173e556146f/. gov/FlexStreets. State legislation could make parklets permanent Senate Bill 314, proposed in the state legislature by Sen. Scott Wiener [D-San Francisco] and called the Bar and Restaurant Recovery Act, proposes several amendments to California’s liquor laws that intend to make them more flexible. If passed, some parklets would become permanent, also meaning restaurants would have the ability to serve alcohol on sidewalks and parking lots. “This expanded outdoor seating and service area – previously prohibited under California’s alcohol laws – has allowed restaurants and bars to survive and has been wildly popular with the public, with a more European-feeling street life,” said Wiener. The bill would also make it easier for bars and restaurants to share commercial, outdoor space with each other, and music venues would no longer need to have full kitchens in order to obtain a liquor license. SB 314 passed unanimously in committee in April, and enjoys bi-partisan support. It is co-authored by Sen. Andreas Borgeas (R-Fresno) and Sen. Jim Nielsen (R-Red Bluff). To learn more about Oakland flex streets program, call 510- 238-7398 or visit OaklandCA. Oakland City Council has agreed to extend its “Flex Streets” parklet program. articles.text: Penelope Sullivan will retire after 27 years teaching 6th grade core and 34 years total in education. Penelope Sullivan has announced her retirement from teaching at Piedmont Middle School, where she has taught sixth grade core for 27 years. A tireless worker who taught for the love of the kids, Sullivan rarely took a day off. She retires in 2021 with more than one year’s worth of untouched sick leave. Sullivan knew early on that she was meant to teach. “I always wanted to be a teacher. As a teenager I worked as an au pair and would go to Tahoe with families for months in the summertime. I just loved being with kids. So, I always thought, gosh, it would just be great to be a teacher.” she said. In college, a 20-year old Penelope called home and said she was thinking of changing her major to focus on becoming a teacher, however the home front was not in favor of the profession. As any good daughter would, Penelope considered the advice. “I immediately said okay, well, I am not going to do that. So, I went the roundabout way. I went to New York to work in advertising, Colorado for retail, then worked at USF as a recruiter.” At age 40 Sullivan became a single mom in Piedmont with two sons at Wildwood and realized she needed to go back to work and rekindle the passion of teaching. Sullivan began as a teacher’s aide in 1987 for Jade Shirachi’s 2nd grade class at Wildwood. After five years, Sullivan got her teaching credential and became a student teacher at Crocker Highlands Elementary at the kindergarten and 4th grade levels. In 1994 three 6th grade positions opened at Piedmont Middle School. That year, PMS found three stalwart teachers who became anchors of the school – Ted Scherman, Hannah Bjork and Penelope Sullivan. On the first day of school Principal John Morrison came into Sullivan’s classroom and said “Okay, I just hired you over the Teacher of the Year in Oakland; so you had better be good.” In her first year teaching full-time, Sullivan knew she could only do one thing: work as hard as she could. Sullivan’s work ethic followed a philosophy of leading by example. She became known as the teacher “who gave the most homework.” But in turn, she invested enormous amounts of her time into grading that homework and made Room 108 into a nurturing home for students for nearly three decades. “To offset the homework reputation, I also became the teacher with the lollipops,” said Sullivan with a grin. Some pieces of her curriculum were best left for a quiet space at home. Her students memorized 9-10 classic pieces of poetry a year, such as Jabberwocky, The Road Not Taken, and Oh Captain, My Captain. Her students also took on the task of creating their own magazines. Each wrote on a topic of their choice – sports, entertainment, food, pop culture – and finished with a piece of original literature. Penelope Sullivan’s Teaching Career • 1987 - 1991 Teacher’s Aide in Jade Shirachi’s 2nd grade class at Wildwood • 1992 Student Teacher Kindergarten and 4th grade at Crocker Highlands • 1993 Teacher’s Aide in Eileen Blood-Golden’s Home Base Class (grades 6-8) at PMS • 1994 - 2021 6th Grade Core Teacher at PMS; also Drama, Communications, Art, and Study Skills • 7th Grade Reading, 7th Grade ASB, Scots Camp, 6th Grade Boot Camp; • Summer School (every year): Welcome to Middle School, Cooking, Watercoloor, Book Making Sullivan said she loved teaching Social Studies most of all, using project-based learning to teach about the Early Hominids, Egypt, India, and China. She is well known at the school (and among faculty members) for leading her class to win the popular Greek Olympics nearly every year. She leaves PMS on top, with her class having won the Greek Olympics five years in a row. “During the John Morrison, Carol King, Brooke Zimmerman era I learned the craft of teaching from experts. There were then and still are exceptional teachers like Stella Kennedy, Marie Cartusciello and so many more. To walk in their shadows was amazing,” said Sullivan. Sullivan taught math by creating a student-run restaurant in her classroom, giving lessons on sales tax and percentages as a cook, cashier and patron. Every year Sullivan also taught summer school including the introductory class, Welcome to Middle School, in addition to Cooking, Water Color, and Book Making. Along with 6th grade teacher Ted Scherman, Sullivan pioneered the orientation programs Scots Camp and 6th Grade Boot Camp to help entering 6th graders feel comfortable on campus through games and team building activities. And now, what’s next for Penelope Sullivan? “I am going to just let things fall into place for the next six months and then make a plan,” she said with a smile. However, she did let on to some potential aspirations: she plans to spend extended periods of time in San Diego with her younger son and grandchildren. After that friends might find her alongside a new four-legged friend. A Bernedoodle tops her list. Or maybe you’ll see her swimming out past the breakers at Stinson Beach.

Engaging in play is an important part of early childhood and contributes to healthy brain development - the benefits are cognitive, physical, social, and emotional. And honestly, it’s good for people of all ages. For children it helps with language, communication, and emotion control. For adults, play reduces stress, and improves brain functionality. And playing together – a departure from the structured segmentation of the pandemic. According to Richard Louv, author of the Last Child in the Woods, playing outside, due to its relatively unstructured nature, also has the added benefit of feeding creativity and imagination. When children spend time playing outside the opportunities to invent, discover, pretend, and problem-solve are bountiful. This kind of break allows children (and adults) to attend to structured participation and formal zoom-room in a much more effective way. articles.text: Big Basin’s Rancho del Oso accessible, Butano opens 5 miles of trails Photo courtesy of California State Parks Portions of Big Basin’s coastal section, Rancho del Oso, has been open to the public since May 23. Two local state parks that were deeply impacted by last year’s CZU Complex Fire have begun a partial reopening. Big Basin’s coastal unit, Rancho del Oso, is now partly accessible, and Butano State Park has officially opened five miles of trails. Environmental scientist Ryan Diller explained the sensitivity of the matter and what needs to occur for the parks to become fully sustainable: “Right now, Big Basin is in a recovery stage,” said Diller, via Big Basin State Park’s Facebook. “It’s experienced a traumatic fire and its immune system is completely gone. That immune system consists of the canopy and the thick duff and litter layer, both in some areas of the park are absent. The duff has been cooked down to bare mineral soil, the canopy has been torched to the point where there’s more light reaching the forest floor since the initial logging industry… We’re excited for the public to come re-enter out parks but a lot of our parks aren’t going to be opening all at once.” Diller confirmed that Rancho del Oso has been partially open since May 30. Waddell Beach and its parking lot are accessible, and its Nature and History Center are open on weekends from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. The Marsh Trail is the only trail available. “Big Basin is still completely closed except for the Rancho del Oso section of Big Basin. When you do go to that part to the park, we ask that you stay on roads, trails and try to prevent any spread of seeds into the burn area,” said Diller. Big Basin Redwoods State Park still has some hotspots popping up. A total of 13 additional burns have recently been addressed by CalFire. “We are not in the clear yet. Impacted areas still contain active fire hazards. [In June] CalFire responded to the Pine Fire which burned 3.7 acres of oldgrowth redwood forest. CalFire identified 11 additional hot spots and responded to a separate 11.5- acre fire within Big Basin,” wrote Big Basin in a recent statement. Butano State Park’s five miles of trails includes portions of: Six Bridges Trail, Jackson Flats Trail, Butano Fire Road Mill Ox Trail, Olmo Fire Road, Goat Hill Trail, and Ben Ries Trail. “At Butano State Park, we’re still clearing roads and trails. It’s a very sensitive time in the recovery period,” said Diller. “Many areas of Butano State Park will remain closed, including the campground. The fire has left many trees compromised and other trail hazards exist, but crews are continuing to work on repairs. For your safety and the health of our park, please stay out of closed areas.” Parking and picnic areas are open, however, TRAIL CLOSURE NOTICE Due to the CZU Fire, areas of Butano State Park will remain Photo courtesy of Youtube. Butano State Park announced last month that it has opened five miles of hiking trails.

Big Basin’s coastal unit, Rancho del Oso, is now partly accessible, and Butano State Park has officially opened five miles of trails. Environmental scientist Ryan Diller explained the sensitivity of the matter and what needs to occur for the parks to become fully sustainable: “Right now, Big Basin is in a recovery stage,” said Diller, via Big Basin State Park’s Facebook. “It’s experienced a traumatic fire and its immune system is completely gone. That immune system consists of the canopy and the thick duff and litter layer, both in some areas of the park are absent. The duff has been cooked down to bare mineral soil, the canopy has been torched to the point where there’s more light reaching the forest floor since the initial logging industry… We’re excited for the public to come re-enter out parks but a lot of our parks aren’t going to be opening all at once.” Diller confirmed that Rancho del Oso has been partially open since May 30. Waddell Beach and its parking lot are accessible, and its Nature and History Center are open on weekends from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. The Marsh Trail is the only trail available. “Big Basin is still completely closed except for the Rancho del Oso section of Big Basin. When you do go to that part to the park, we ask that you stay on roads, trails and try to prevent any spread of seeds into the burn area,” said Diller. Impacted areas still contain active fire hazards. [In June] CalFire responded to the Pine Fire which burned 3.7 acres of oldgrowth redwood forest. CalFire identified 11 additional hot spots and responded to a separate 11.5- acre fire within Big Basin,” wrote Big Basin in a recent statement. Butano State Park’s five miles of trails includes portions of: Six Bridges Trail, Jackson Flats Trail, Butano Fire Road Mill Ox Trail, Olmo Fire Road, Goat Hill Trail, and Ben Ries Trail. “At Butano State Park, we’re still clearing roads and trails. It’s a very sensitive time in the recovery period,” said Diller. “Many areas of Butano State Park will remain closed, including the campground. articles.text: The CONCACAF Gold Cup soccer tournament returns this week with three group stage matches starting on Saturday, July 10. The tournament runs through July 18, with quarterfinals on July 24, semifinals on July 29, and championship round on August 1. articles.text: We last visited Huckleberry Botanic Regional Preserve in the Oakland Hills in May 2020 on a rainy morning. The park is noted for its year-round display of blossoming flowers on its easy 2.4-mile loop, and even in the dry months of summer there are some plants on exhibit. Hikers are in closer contact with foliage than perhaps any other trail in the Oakland hills. In July you will see western bracken, coastal wood, and western sword ferns. The trail passes underneath moss-covered California Bay Laurels trees, with shoots sprouting from downed trees. Giant cape ivy leaves line a portion of the narrow trail as they thrive in the summer sun. Another section of brittleleaf Manzanita shows its distinct redbark beginning to crack and warp in the dry heat. You can find yellow monkeyflowers on the lower portion of the Huckleberry Botanic loop, in addition to a segment of California aralia, which has a low-hanging canopy of enormously large leaves. The sheer size of the leafy lush-green verdant area is mesmerizing. Yellow monkey flowers are currently in bloom. Ferns of different species surround hikers at Huckleberry Botanic, with informative panels describing the abundant foliage. California Bay Laurels surround hikers on this shady trail. Stay on the path to the right to continue on the full 2.4-mile loop.

articles.text: Andre Thierry, a Richmond-native with strong Louisiana Zydeco influences, is one of this year’s featured performers. The Yerba Buena Gardens Festival is free, with live music and performances through August 28. For over two decades, Yerba Buena Gardens Festival has presented free outdoor music, circus, dance, poetry, theatre, and youth programs by artists from the Bay Area and around the world. The festival was cancelled last year due to the COVID-19 pandemic. The festival opened this summer on June 26 with a concert by Bobi Cespedes, the “matriarch of Cuban roots in the Bay Area.” July highlights include the first of a three-part series of dance events by the Yerba Buena Gardens ChoreoFest, music by Zydeco musician Andre Thierry, and Oakland-based hip-hop orchestra Ensemble Mik Nawooj. Children’s programs in July include Pi Clowns and Red Panda Acrobats. In addition to a long list of Afro-Cuban, jazz, Zydeco, and ensemble offerings, the festival also features outdoor dance classes and American Native dance presentations. “I could not be more thrilled to announce this special Festival season of free performances and concerts this summer,” said Festival Artistic Director Linda Lucero. “I am so excited to welcome everyone back to the beautiful Gardens to experience our region’s rich cultural diversity and the immense fortitude of our local artists and performers. After a long period of isolation for many of us, Yerba Buena Gardens Festival remains a space for art and joy, welcoming people from all walks of life. There’s nothing that gladdens the heart and spirit more than celebrating the performing arts together under open skies,” she said. The Yerba Buena Gardens is located on Mission Street between 3rd and 4th streets in San Francisco. Visit www.ybgfestival.org for full schedule. ®
articles.title: Yerba Buena Festival continues through August

articles.text: A “Sculpture Show Evening Stroll” will be held tomorrow, Thursday, July 8 at the Ruth Bancroft Garden in Walnut Creek. It will feature the works of over 20 renowned Northern California artists. Each year the garden’s art show and sale showcases sculptural art using the natural backdrop of the location. Live jazz music from the band Four and More will be performed, and beer and wine will be available for purchase. A special members-only after-hours evening sculpture stroll begins at 5 p.m. The Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery is famous for its extensive collection of succulents, cacti, California native plants, and other drought-tolerant plants. The garden was originally planted in 1972 by Ruth Bancroft when it was her private, personal garden but is now open six days a week for the education and enjoyment of the public. Bancroft created a garden filled with dynamic plant combinations using drought-tolerant plants that very few other gardeners were using at the time. In 1989, her garden was selected by the Garden Conservancy to be its first preservation project, and a conservation easement was established to ensure its permanent preservation. Visitors can browse the garden from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., Tuesday through Thursday, and 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Friday through Sunday. For a full list of what’s in bloom, visit https://www.ruthbancroftgarden.org/wp/wp-content/uploads/Whats-In-BloomJuly-2021.pdf. To plan your visit to the gardens, go to the organization’s homepage: https://www. ruthbancroftgarden.org/.
articles.title: Ruth Bancroft Garden hosts annual “Sculpture Show Evening Stroll” tomorrow

articles.text: Music@Menlo returns this summer with a mix of in-person and digital performances beginning on July 16. The 2021 season, entitled “Gather,” will take place in and around the festival’s new $40 million Spieker Center for the Arts on the campus of Menlo School in Menlo Park. Music@Menlo is an internationally acclaimed chamber music festival founded by David Finckel and Wu Han. Inaugurated in 2003 at Menlo School, the festival features concerts, lectures, and a training program for aspiring professional musicians. This year’s events will be smaller in size than its 18 previous seasons but will continue to include a star-studded lineup of musicians. The festival will include a mix of live and digitally-streamed performances between July 16 and August 1. Featured concerts will be performed at 4 p.m. on Friday, Saturday, and Sunday in the Spieker Center, and then repeated at 6 p.m. outdoors. Concerts will run for approximately one hour without intermission. There will be nine main concerts grouped over three weekends. The season-opening concert on July 16 includes the world premiere of Patrick Castillo’s Gather, a new work commissioned for the festival’s new home at Spieker Center. Castillo has held a variety of positions with the festival since its inception. He was recently named the New York Philharmonic’s Vice President of Artistic Planning. “I was honored to be asked by David and Wu Han to create a new piece to celebrate the opening of Music at Menlo’s new concert hall. This is a compelling techno-thriller that should ring true, especially for the twenty-something moviegoers. They get what happened to Sony. Starring Chris Hemsworth, Viola Davis, Wei Tang. 2 hrs., 14 min. Rated R. George Clooney and Jack O’Connell star in Money Monster. Money Monster is a close facsimile of CNBC’s Mad Money with Jim Cramer. Consider it a parody (at least initially) of the show with a sprinkling of satire. Lee Gates (George Clooney) is the show’s host, an insouciant dispenser of stock tips and financial advice, offered up more as entertainment than as substantive analysis of the market and why some stocks are nuggets and others are to be avoided. What Lee – narcissistic, pampered and glib – has forgotten is that there are those in his audience who listen closely and take his shtick seriously. Case in point is Kyle Budwell (Jack O’Connell), a working stiff whose mom has died and left him some $60k that he invests in a financial outfit named Ibis Clear Capital – at the suggestion of Lee. Kyle shows up at the beginning of Lee’s show to ask Lee why his nest egg has vanished, only he’s got a gun and a suicide vest, which he insists that Lee put on. Let’s say that rage and revenge are Kyle’s default settings. What he wants is an explanation. What happened that caused his stock to tank? If he doesn’t get some answers, he’s going to turn Lee into mist. The deal is that he makes $14 per hour at his delivery job and can’t afford to keep himself or his girlfriend above water. The $60k represented hope. In the control room, suddenly faced with a chaotic hostage situation, is Patty Fenn (Julia Roberts), Lee’s producer, who is talking to him via his earpiece. And it’s Patty who begins working furiously to get some backstory on the company that tanked – what happened to cause the company to suddenly lose $800 million. Since the CEO, Walt Camby (Dominic West) is unavailable – in a corporate jet somewhere over the Atlantic – she’s talking to the company’s PR head, Diane Lester (Caitriona Balfe), who is not very helpful. So there is the triangle squared: Lee, facing a very angry investor, Kyle ready to shoot Lee or blow him up, Patty in the control room, talking to Lee and Diane. There is, of course, a serious response by the New York police who want to shoot Kyle, but not as long as he’s holding the dead man’s trigger connected to the vest. Consider all of the above as act one. What follows serves only to ratchet up the tension. The mystery of what happened to the $800 million is incrementally sorted out with a math guy in Seoul explaining financial algorithms and stock fluctuations, a couple of laid-back hackers in Reykjavik who are happy to be in the game, and later the CEO pf the company who was in South Africa working his side of the street. Meanwhile Lee and Kyle are in the studio and Patty is in the control room trying to manage what is uncontrollable, hoping to keep Kyle from having a meltdown while pointing a gun at Lee’s head. And thus begins act three. Is Money Monster entertaining? Yes. But then it’s got a deep bench of talent, starting with Clooney and Roberts. And the writing is good, at times gripping. Though it relies on some financial arcana, it doesn’t take the audience so deep into the weeds that the details can seem unintelligible, such as The Big Short. But there are moments when the collective villain is Wall Street with its casino-like approach to investing, to include their esoteric financial instruments. Meanwhile, Kyle represents the victims. But still, with Jodie Foster at the helm, this is good summer entertainment. Money Monster. Directed by Jodie Foster. Starring George Clooney, Julia Roberts, Jack O’Connell. 1 hr., 38 min. Rated R.

Let’s say that rage and revenge are Kyle’s default settings. What he wants is an explanation. What happened that caused his stock to tank? If he doesn’t get some answers, he’s going to turn Lee into mist. The deal is that he makes $14 per hour at his delivery job and can’t afford to keep himself or his girlfriend above water. The $60k represented hope. In the control room, suddenly faced with a chaotic hostage situation, is Patty Fenn (Julia Roberts), Lee’s producer, who is talking to him via his earpiece. And it’s Patty who begins working furiously to get some backstory on the company that tanked – what happened to cause the company to suddenly lose $800 million. Since the CEO, Walt Camby (Dominic West) is unavailable – in a corporate jet somewhere over the Atlantic – she’s talking to the company’s PR head, Diane Lester (Caitriona Balfe), who is not very helpful. So there is the triangle squared: Lee, facing a very angry investor, Kyle ready to shoot Lee or blow him up, Patty in the control room, talking to Lee and Diane. There is, of course, a serious response by the New York police who want to shoot Kyle, but not as long as he’s holding the dead man’s trigger connected to the vest. Consider all of the above as act one. What follows serves only to ratchet up the tension. The mystery of what happened to the $800 million is incrementally sorted out with a math guy in Seoul explaining financial algorithms and stock fluctuations, a couple of laid-back hackers in Reykjavik who are happy to be in the game, and later the CEO pf the company who was in South Africa working his side of the street. Meanwhile Lee and Kyle are in the studio and Patty is in the control room trying to manage what is uncontrollable, hoping to keep Kyle from having a meltdown while pointing a gun at Lee’s head. And thus begins act three. Is Money Monster entertaining? Yes. But then it’s got a deep bench of talent, starting with Clooney and Roberts. And the writing is good, at times gripping. Though it relies on some financial arcana, it doesn’t take the audience so deep into the weeds that the details can seem unintelligible, such as The Big Short. But there are moments when the collective villain is Wall Street with its casino-like approach to investing, to include their esoteric financial instruments. Meanwhile, Kyle represents the victims. But still, with Jodie Foster at the helm, this is good summer entertainment. Money Monster. Directed by Jodie Foster. Starring George Clooney, Julia Roberts, Jack O’Connell. 1 hr., 38 min. Rated R. articles.text: Luke Bernard (center) as Billy Forrester in How to Eat Fried Worms. A film based on the Thomas Rockwell book. First things first: How to Eat Fried Worms, based on the Thomas Rockwell book, is a gross-out delight. Its target audience is kids 6 to 11, who will find the story definitely cringe-worthy, but in a good way. If you’ve spent any time hanging out with youngsters, you know that they relish saying “eeewwww!” Or, “that is so disgusting!” The story revolves around Billy Forrester (Luke Bernard), 11-years-old, who is about to start a new school. In other words, he will have to endure the new kid syndrome: short on friends with not a clue how to get around. As it turns out, there are a few kids who reach out to him; however, they hang out on the fringe and are considered uncool. There’s Erika (Halle Kate Eisenberg), also known as “Erk”, tall and gangly and definitely not one of the popular kids. And there’s Adam (Austin Rogers) who, like Erika, carries the tag of “loser.” Unfortunately, Billy draws the attention not only of the marginal kids, but of Joe (Adam Hicks), school bully, and his toadies Plug (Blake Garrett), and Bradley (Phillip Daniel Bolden). Unbeknownst to Billy, they steal his lunchbox, then return it, and then during lunch, when Billy pours out what he expects will be milk from his thermos, he discovers it’s filled with worms. Billy, who has a sensitive stomach, comes close to vomiting at the first sight of the night crawlers. After school, on his way home, Billy runs into Joe and his gang. Joe asks him how he liked the worms. Billy says they’re great and he eats them all the time. Joe says, “oh yeah?” And Billy says “Really.” And that’s when Joe challenges him to a bet: if Billy can eat 10 worms without throwing up, Joe will come to School with a mess of worms in his pants. If he can’t, then it’s Billy who has to come to school with worms in his shorts. Foolishly, Billy, who feels he can’t back down, looks at Joe and accepts. Sure. No problem. The next day, determined, Billy begins cooking and frying all manner of worms. There’s “Le Porker,” “The Greasy Brown Toad Boater,” “The Burning Fishbait” and so on. Billy eats them one by one, some microwaved, spread with peanut butter, or hidden in marshmallows. The question is, will Billy finish all ten, or miss Joe’s deadline. It’s going to be close. Which is what makes How to Eat Fried Worms grossly fun. How to Eat Fried Worms. Live action. Directed by Bob Dolman. Starring Luke Bernard, Tom Cavanaugh, Kimberly Williams-Paisley. 1 hr., 24 min. Rated PG.

articles.text: Disney’s remake of its 1998 animated feature, Mulan, is now live action, told on a grand scale, reportedly costing some $200 million. It’s an epic saga, based on a 400-year-old folk song that describes a young woman, Mulan (Yifei Liu), who, when her ailing father is drafted as part of the emperor’s call to arms, makes the extraordinary decision to take her father’s place, disguised as a man. Wearing her father’s armor, with her chest bound with cloth, she manages to pass the test of her disguise, and is accepted as one of the thousands of conscripted warriors preparing for battle. It’s at this point that the narrative becomes a simply told tale, one of spectacular battles and desperate survival with a touch of slow-motion magic. It’s during these head-on confrontations with the northern nomads that we come to realize that Mulan possesses not only uncommon bravery, but dazzling skills that allow her to defy gravity. As part of understanding her ability to all but fly, while performing unexpected balletic twists and turns, we learn that she possesses what is referred to as “chi,” a remarkable and essential life force (think of the “Force” in Star Wars). Mulan’s ch’i is exceptional, allowing her to slow down time, all while performing perfect kicks and turns. The only thing that diminishes Mulan’s ch’i is the fact that she is also perpetrating a dishonesty, one she must not reveal. What she is must remain hidden. Her main adversary is not the shape-shifting witch Xianniang (Gong Li), who has a falcon’s claw for a hand, and is formidable in every way; rather, Mulan must confront Boris Khan (Jason Scott Lee), leader of the northern cohort, a distinguished warrior who has grievances with the emperor. It is part of Mulan’s mission, part of her honor, to protect the emperor. At the center of this compelling tale is an amazing, heroic, empowered young woman who displays not only bravery but loyalty and truth – and all while living a lie. She struggles with her gender-bending identity and it is this tension that carries the film to that remarkable moment when she finally steps forward and reveals who she truly is. Mulan. A Disney live action feature. Directed by Niki Caro. Starring Yifei Liu, Donnie Yen Ji-Dan, Jason Scott Lee. 1 hr., 56 min. Rated PG-13. A scene from Disney’s live action feature, Mulan.

articles.text: Composer Jake Heggie By Allyson Aleksey Festival Opera’s 30th anniversary season continues with the world premiere of A Jake Heggie Triptych featuring the award-winning composer. Live performances will be held on August 13 and August 15, both at the Hofmann Theatre at Lesher Center for the Arts in Walnut Creek. Directed by Mark Foehringer and conducted by Bryan Nies, with members of the Festival Opera Orchestra, Heggie will be joined by Gene Scheer as well as acclaimed singers Carrie Hennessey, Diana Tash, award-winning actor Curt Branom and Festival Opera General Director Zachary Gordin. The world premiere event of works by Heggie features three song cycles, reimagined as fully staged chamber operas. The Triptych is the result of Gordin’s long relationship with Heggie and his works. “I’ve been a huge fan of Jake’s work since the release of his “The Faces of Love” album in 1999, which featured many dear colleagues and friends. I was immediately struck by his ability to build a whole environment with his piano writing, and how operatic in nature it is. The music provides both an orchestra and scenery,” Gordin said. “As a singer who is always looking for the essential truth in the music and stories I’m telling, it was a revelation to see his vocal writing truly mirroring the inflection, joy, and pathos of the human voice with honesty, setting texts in an immediately accessible, and deeply compelling way.” “I’m deeply honored that Festival Opera will present this dynamic triptych of my compositions, beautifully cast with stunning performers,” Heggie said. “The human quest for identity and connection links this trio of works, which were created with my most frequent collaborators – Gene Scheer and the late, great American playwright Terrence McNally. What a dream for this to unfold in the East Bay, where long ago I studied piano as a teenager.” Triptych will have two live performances, on Friday, August 13 at 7:30 p.m., and Sunday, August 15 at 2:00 p.m. in the Hofmann Theatre at the Lesher Center for the Arts. Tickets are on sale now and can be purchased by visiting https://www.festivalopera.org/a-jake-heggie-triptych.

articles.text: Les Cadrans de Lassegue a Bargain Bordeaux As you know, Pierre’s motto has always been any idiot with a hundred bucks can buy a good wine. It takes knowledge and skill to buy a good one for $15. In the world of Bordeaux, wine price escalation has made it pretty impossible to buy a good one for $15, Thus week’s wine, which retails for $30, is a true bargain. When the wines of Bordeaux were classified into a five-tier ranking in 1855, they concentrated solely on the wines of the left bank, the Medoc area. Those were the wines that gained fame and prestige over the years. The wines of the “Right Bank” like Pomerol and St. Emillion were shunted off to the side. But today many of these estates have gained fame and notoriety. One of the world’s most expensive wines, Petrus, is grown here. But by in large, the Right Bank is the place to look for bargains in Bordeaux. The main grape is Merlot often blended with Cabernet Franc. The soil has much more clay than the gravelly land of the Medoc, giving the grapes a soft richness and mellowing the tannins. Chateau Lassegue is a beautiful estate in the heart of St. Emillion region. Recently they decided to make a second wine they named Les Cadrans de Lassegue, a blend of 90% Merlot and 10% Cabernet Franc, designed to showcase a more elegant, finesse style of wine.

articles.text: Fresh Strawberry Cobbler Strawberry fields stretch seemingly forever along Monterey Bay, which means we have a plentiful supply of multiple varieties at our local farmer’s markets. In fact, the majority of strawberries finding their way to American tables come from our California Coastal fields. Strawberry cobbler brings the flavors of strawberry shortcake in a simpler preparation than making individual shortcakes for the same number of servings. It’s also heartier for transport and serving at summer BBQs and picnics. A few advance tips 1. Make sure the butter and heavy cream are well chilled. You can also pre-chill the mixing bowl in the freezer if your kitchen is warm. 2. Keep the balls of dough on the smaller side, and don’t overcrowd them. articles.text: Marianne Mitosinka Many gardeners know that pesticides are harmful to the environment and try to minimize their use, but did you know that many of the plants that you buy come pretreated with pesticides called neonicotinoids (neonics)? Neonics are derived from nicotine, and these pesticides contaminate the entire plant for at least 10 years, as well as the soil in which they are planted, the water they come in contact with, and the insects and pollinators that feed on them. According to the Pollinator Posse (www.pollinatorposse.org), plants treated with neonics may be more attractive to pollinators like bees, which may amplify their harmful ecological impact. Neonics are considered a primary contributor to the massive decrease in bee and monarch butterfly populations, along with climate change and habitat loss. Perhaps more alarming, neonics are also linked to nervous system toxicity and reproductive disorders in humans. What can you do? When purchasing plants, read the plant label carefully or ask if they have been treated with neonics. Let proprietors know that you prefer untreated plants. If in doubt, shop elsewhere. Native plants are typically grown by A native bumblebee relishing this long-blooming California-native Yellow Bush Lupine in a front garden in Piedmont. specialist native plant nurseries that do not use neonics. Luckily, Inner East Bay gardeners have several neonic-free native nurseries nearby: East Bay Wilds Native Plant Nursery (www. eastbaywilds.com) in Oakland; Native Here Nursery (www. nativeherenursery.org) in Berkeley; Oaktown Native Plant Nursery (www.oaktownnursery.com) in Berkeley; and The Watershed Nursery (www.watershednursery. com) in Richmond. Ace Garden Center on Grand Ave. carries some (but not all) neonic-free brands; their native plant section is quite small. A more complete list of Bay Area native plant nurseries is available at: https://www.bringingbackthenatives.net/find-a-nursery. California is currently considering whether to list neonics under Proposition 65, based on neurodevelopmental and reproductive effects on humans. In the world of Bordeaux, wine price escalation has made it pretty impossible to buy a good one for $15, Thus week’s wine, which retails for $30, is a true bargain. When the wines of Bordeaux were classified into a five-tier ranking in 1855, they concentrated solely on the wines of the left bank, the Medoc area. But today many of these estates have gained fame and notoriety. One of the world’s most expensive wines, Petrus, is grown here. But by in large, the Right Bank is the place to look for bargains in Bordeaux. The main grape is Merlot often blended with Cabernet Franc. The soil has much more clay than the gravelly land of the Medoc, giving the grapes a soft richness and mellowing the tannins. Chateau Lassegue is a beautiful estate in the heart of St. Emillion region. Recently they decided to make a second wine they named Les Cadrans de Lassegue, a blend of 90% Merlot and 10% Cabernet Franc, designed to showcase a more elegant, finesse style of wine. articles.text: Here’s something to think about: You could spend two, or even three, decades in retirement. To meet your income needs for all those years, you’ll generally need a sizable amount of retirement assets. How will Social Security fit into the picture? For most people, Social Security won’t be enough to cover the cost of living in retirement. Nonetheless, Social Security benefits are still valuable, so you’ll want to do whatever you can to maximize them. Your first move is to determine when you should start taking Social Security. You can begin collecting benefits when you reach 62 – but should you? If you were to turn 62 this year, your payments would only be about 71% of what you’d get if you waited until your full retirement age, which is 66 years and 10 months. (“Full retirement age” varies, depending on when you were born, but for most people today, it will be between 66 and 67.) Every month you wait between now and your full retirement age, your benefits will increase. If you still want to delay taking benefits beyond your full retirement age, your payments will increase by 8% each year, until you’re 70, when they “max out.” Regardless of when you file, you’ll also receive an annual costof-living adjustment. So, when should you start claiming your benefits? There’s no one “right” answer for everyone. If you turn 62 and you need the money, your choice might be made for you. But if you have sufficient income from other sources, you’re in good health and you have longevity in your family, or you’re still working, it might be worthwhile to wait until your full retirement age, or perhaps even longer, to start collecting. Another key consideration is spousal benefits. If your own full retirement benefit is less than 50% of your spouse’s full retirement benefit, you would generally be eligible to claim spousal benefits, provided you’re at least 62 and your spouse has filed for Social Security benefits. Survivor benefits are another important consideration. When you pass away, your spouse would be able to receive up to 100% of your benefit or his/her own retirement benefit, whichever is higher. Thus, delaying Social Security could not only increase your own benefit, but also the benefit for your surviving spouse. An additional issue to think about, when planning for how Social Security fits into your retirement, is your earned income. If you’re younger than full retirement age, your benefit will be reduced by $1 for each $2 you earn above a certain amount, which, in 2021, is $18,960. During the year you reach full retirement age, your benefit will be reduced by $1 for each $3 you earn above a set amount ($50,520 in 2021). But once you hit the month at which you attain full retirement age, and from that point on, you can keep all of your benefits, no matter how much you earn (although your benefits could still be taxed). One final point to keep in mind: The more you accumulate in your other retirement accounts, such as your IRA and 401(k) or similar employer-sponsored plan, the more flexibility you’ll have in managing your Social Security benefits. So, throughout your working years, try to contribute as much as you can afford to these plans. This article was written by Edward Jones for use by your local Edward Jones Financial Advisor. T.J. articles.text: A large group of Wednesday Walkers paused to take a photo before heading to Grand Avenue, Pictured are Priscilla Wanerus (left), Alicia Rivera, Jim Kuo, Alan Goldhammer, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Cat Gustafson, Bob Gustafson, Eva Phalen, Albert Chen, Chelle Putzer, Swee Ling Chen, Ellen Beilock, Sara Engel, Melba Yee, Sarah Johnson, Nadine Guffanti, Nancy Olsen, Quincy Dong, Susan Martin, Helen Dong, Stella Houston, Noemi Alvarado, Haybert Houston, Sherry Jacobs, Harriette Louie, Iris Hudis, Barry Gantt, Brenda Ferrero, and Fia Hsu. It was a cool, overcast morning on June 30 when the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesday group assembled at the Exedra. The weather was great for walking and helped bring out a strong showing of 29 walkers and two special guests. Piedmont Recreation Director Chelle Putzer was there to introduce new Recreation Supervisor Eva Phalen to the group. Chelle and Eva worked together at the Albany Recreation Department, and Eva told the group a little more about her background and desires for programing in Piedmont. The group was also pleased to welcome first-time walkers Sara Engel and Ellen Beilock. Drawing on Gail Lombardi’s Piedmont Historical Society articles in the Post, the walkers learned about the commercial history of Grand Avenue. In 1929 the Piedmont City Council adopted an ordinance that allowed businesses on the west side of the street from the Oakland city line at Wildwood Avenue to Linda Avenue, and also on the east side of the street to Fairview Avenue. Seven months later, voters rejected extending the business district to Oakland Avenue, and it remains the same to this day. Going down Magnolia Avenue, the group took a side trip on Jerome Avenue to see Keefer Court, a cul-de-sac that has homes with wonderfully unique, cactus front yard gardens. Dick Carter introduced himself to a resident, only to discover it was Ginny Hart Wright, a Piedmont High classmate of Dick’s. Ginny told the group that a number of years back the son of one of the homeowners replaced his parents’ front yard plants with what is now a beautiful cactus garden. The walkers went to Grand Avenue, and at the corner of Grand and Linda, the history of the city’s earliest businesses at the site was told from Gail Lombardi’s article. In 1892 Axel R. Gruggel built a restaurant at this corner and called it A Mon Chateau (My Castle). He also had a beer garden in the back on the Linda Avenue side of the restaurant. From 1903 on, the restaurant had a series of owners and issues. In 1907 three bachelors operated it and lived on the second floor. They sold wine, liquor, and cigars in addition to dinners, and the neighbors didn’t like all the noise. In 1907 the new City of Piedmont passed liquor licensing regulations, and when the bachelors applied for a license they were denied. However, they continued to sell liquor and in 1908 they were arrested and their liquor was confiscated. In 1911 a new owner changed the restaurant into “The Piedmont Casino.” In two rooms upstairs patrons played poker and faro, but gambling was illegal. The casino was raided in 1912 and nine card-players were arrested and each fined $55. Not surprisingly, the casino closed soon after. In 1914 the restaurant’s building become the Grand Avenue Grocery Company, and in 1922 the Del Monte Market. They did well, but later Piggly Wiggly opened a supermarket just down the street at Sunnyside and Grand. It was tough competition and the Del Monte Market closed in 1935. The old A Mon Chateau building was torn down in 1936 and the Richfield Oil Company built a gas station on the site. Other gas station companies later owned the site. In 1987 Chevron sold the property, and the current two-story Piedmont Financial Center was built there. The large group crossed Grand Avenue at Ace Hardware, stopping a good number of cars in the process. They went up Wildwood Avenue to Palm Drive, where Sherry Jacobs pointed out a home on Magnolia Avenue that was once a summer home of the Coit family of San Francisco tower fame. It had been an almost three-mile walk in an hour and a half with interesting history and friends on a pleasant morning. The group invited Phalen to join them on future walks. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation is required by contacting John Wilk at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. articles.text: The American Red Cross continues to experience a severe blood shortage. Blood and platelet donors are needed now to help ensure hospital shelves are stocked with blood products. As a thank-you, donors who donate blood between July 7-31 will receive a $10 Amazon.com gift card by email, plus a chance to win gas for one year (a $5,000 value). Donors of all blood types – especially type O and those giving platelets – are urged to make an appointment to give now by using the Red Cross Blood Donor App, visiting RedCrossBlood. org, or calling 1-800-RED CROSS (1-800-733-2767). The Red Cross is working around the clock to provide blood products to hospitals responding to an unusually high number of traumas and emergency room visits, as well as overdoses and resulting transplants. As a result of the blood shortage, some hospitals are being forced to slow the pace of elective surgeries until the blood supply stabilizes, delaying crucial patient care. To donate blood, call the Oakland Blood Bank, 6230 Claremont Avenue, at 800-733-2767. This week, the blood bank is open 12:15 p.m. - 7:00 p.m. Monday - Wednesday 10:45 a.m. - 5:30 p.m. Thursday 7:45 a.m. - 2:30 p.m. Friday - Sunday To donate blood, individuals need to bring a driver’s license or their blood donor card. Individuals aged 17 who weigh at least 110 pounds and are in good health may be eligible to donate blood.

articles.text: KQED, Northern California’s National Public Radio (NPR) station, has announced an allday block party on September 25 to celebrate its newly-designed headquarters on Mariposa Street. The newly renovated-headquarters transforms the office building from industrial-style to an accessible, state-of-theart center. It was designed by the award-winning San Francisco-based architecture firm EHDD. The station purchased the building in 1991, when KQED’s primary focus was television and radio production. Presently, KQED serves audiences on broadcast as well as through digital media tools like social media and web, podcasts, and live and virtual events. Since 1991, the station’s staff has doubled and its content services have expanded. It is now home to one of the largest newsrooms in California. “KQED will redefine public media for the Bay Area, making it more diverse, participatory and community powered,” said Michael Isip, KQED President and CEO. “The new headquarters will enable our staff to thrive in providing crucial programming and education services and will expand possibilities for our community to come together to find common ground.” The new design features modernized production and studio spaces, expanding KQED’s ability to provide quality digital programming. EHDD’s design also increases visibility to the public; a new corner entry at Mariposa and Bryant Streets establishes a more prominent position in the Mission Street neighborhood with a glass facade. “We’re lifting up the façade to invite the community in,” said Rebecca Sharkey, EHDD Principal. “This new building represents the physical place of KQED engagement, a place to connect face-to-face with journalists and neighbors, to experience the breadth of KQED content, and to engage in dialogue about issues that matter most to the Bay Area and beyond.” KQED Grand Opening KQED will host a free, allday open house and block party on Saturday, September 25, unveiling its newly designed headquarters to the public. The community is invited to participate in an array of live programs and performances, featuring notable guests and radio personalities from KQED, NPR, Public Broadcasting Station (PBS) and PBS kids. There will also be workshops, media-making activities, and family and kid-friendly games throughout the building. “In a protracted time of separation and isolation, we’ve learned how to better use digital tools for virtual dialogue and participation.” Isip said. “We’ll continue to use technology to fill gaps and extend the reach of our work. Bringing people together for personal connection is essential for a strong, vibrant community.” For more information about the block party and open house, visit kqed.org/events.
articles.title: KQED celebrates new HQ with block party Sept. 25

Mary Lu was born Mary Lucille Roberts on August 6, 1940, to Edward and Veronica Roberts in Chicago, Illinois. A proud Chicago Southsider, she always cheered for the White Sox and whoever played against the Cubs. Mary Lu attended Little Flower Grammar School, Maria High School, Mt. Mary College, and Loyola University graduate school. After her year at Loyola, she drove to San Francisco for a job as a social worker with Catholic Charities and settled on Noe Street with three of her college roommates. Soon thereafter, she met her lifelong partner, Dave Lillevand. They wed in 1965 at Mission Delores Basilica and recently celebrated their 56th wedding anniversary. Their two children, Sara Rose and David Edward, were born while they lived on Ascot Drive in Oakland. The family moved to Piedmont in 1974, and the Sotelo house became the focal point for many memorable events, including extended family gatherings, sports team celebrations, school functions, community gatherings, and law firm summer associate parties. Mary Lu was an exceptional hostess and culinary genius who loved bringing people together. During her last days, family and friends from all walks of life shared happy memories of her kindness, generosity, her no-nonsense demeanor and clever humor. Mary Lu and Dave spent the last 19 years together living in Oakland, just one block from the original home on Ascot Drive. After working as a teacher’s aide in Piedmont School District, the Birthday Group, the Gourmet Group, the New Year Eve Pals, the USF Basketball families, the Last Tuesday of the Month Book Club, and the Local Mt. Mary Alumnae. Mary Lu was a lover of food (“not too spicy”), wine, and a nightly Manhattan. She loved to travel and spent countless hours planning trips, including “road scholar” and other educational travel excursions. Indeed, she had a Mississippi River cruise planned for this coming August. She would have been an excellent spy as her eavesdropping skills and ability to read people in social settings were extraordinary, right up to her final breaths. Mary Lu was committed to her Catholic faith which framed her approach to all that came her way, while strongly believing that women should be allowed to become priests. Before the pandemic, she was a regular at Our Lady of Lourdes in Oakland for Sunday Mass. Her strong will, intuition, wit, and open-mindedness also served her well in straightening out life’s curve balls and wrinkles. Mary Lu is survived by her husband Dave, son David, daughter Sara and daughter-in-law Maryann. She was affectionately known as “Grandma LuLu” to grandchildren Kevin, Dominic, Conor, Nicholas, Jacob, Margo and Tucker, and “Auntie Mary” to dozens of nieces, nephews and cousins. She is predeceased by her parents and three siblings, Donald, Jean and David. Her immediate and extended family as well as countless friends will miss her greatly. Time will have a tough assignment to assuage her loss. Private family services will be held. Mary Lu Lillevand, a longtime resident of Piedmont, passed away on June 28. She was 80. Mary Lu earned a teaching credential at Holy Names College and went on to teach 2nd grade at St. Leander’s in San Leandro until retiring to care for her parents in their declining years. Mary Lu’s volunteer efforts are too many to list, but highlights include her time as a docent at the Oakland Museum of California, traveling to classrooms throughout the Bay Area to teach about the Gold Rush, and her many hours at the Bambino Thrift Store raising funds for the Teak Branch of Children’s Hospital in Oakland. In recognition of her efforts, she was one of the first recipients of the Betty C. Howard Award for volunteerism in the City of Piedmont. Mary Lu was a fierce advocate for student participation in athletics with a particular emphasis on gender equity. Mary Lu was instrumental in establishing the right for Millennium High School students to play on Piedmont High School athletic teams. Celebrating July 4th this week brings up the holidays question. Like all cultures that value the tradition of being together while missing loved ones, we treasure our Paris friends, fellow Yanks who are rowing in the same foreign waters that we are. We share, we laugh, we mourn. Thanksgiving of 2019 was the first holiday to pop the question: how do we honor a tradition when our lives are far out of position from what we’ve usually done year to year? articles.text: Part 2 in a series Whisky. The very word invites a smile. Go ahead. Try it. Say “whisky” and watch the upward curve of the lips. Whisky is derived from usky, an eighteenth century adaptation of the Gaelic uisage beatha, which was a translation of the Latin aqua vitae, meaning “water of life.” Is it any wonder, then, that distillers proudly tout malt whisky as the result of a trinity of ingredients: barley, yeast and water? On some lighter, younger whiskies, it is possible to nose out and taste the yeasty cereal notes of the base barley. The real cornucopia of aromas and flavors – the baking spices, honey, vanilla, caramel, toffee, almonds, dried fruits, apple, pear, white flowers, chocolate shavings, ripe banana, coconut, and more – comes from the casks used for maturation. Casks open up a realm of options almost as extensive as the list of characteristics they impart. There are choices on the type of oak, size, degree to which the inside of the cask is toasted and what it was previously used to age. Most frequently, the casks used for whisky contained either bourbon or sherry. Proportions from each would be married together to create the whisky. While following the signposts along the whisky trail in Speyside of Scotland’s eastern Highlands, I quickly learned that the lineup of cask alternatives has been expanding. In the early 2000s, UK law permitted alternative casks, such as those used for brandies and fortified wines, for maturing whisky. Maturing, by definition, can be a slow and lengthy process, and we may now be seeing the results of the tinkering that occurred under a more elastic law. Based on stops for tastings, Port pipes and former cabernet sauvignon barrels seem to be the ones making their way into this mix, bringing in shades of richer fruits such as plum and dark cherry. At Dalmore, the King Alexander III is an elixir that pulls in from six different cask types, including bourbon, sherry, Port and cabernet sauvignon as well as Madeira drums and Malaga barrels. To be sure, casks have always played a central role. Many distilleries are quick to cite that 80 to 85 percent of a whisky’s flavor comes from the casks. Macallan rates the importance of the cask so highly that there is an entirely designated position for selecting the individual trees that will be used to make the casks. From the American oak, which grows taller and has smaller leaves, comes hints of butterscotch and caramel as well as lighter amber and yellow color tones. European oak, which takes longer to grow, imparts the “Christmas cake” (a popular catch-all for describing the combination of spices like nutmeg and dried fruits) and deeper red hues. Given the heavy responsibility of the casks in transmuting barley, yeast and water into the full kaleidoscope that we know as whisky, it seems an oversight to exclude them from the list of ingredients. When asked, I’ve found that the good folks working distilleries will give a nod to casks, but it’s hard to budge them on tradition and the lyricism of holding to the three raw materials. These same aficionados will then lean in and whisper the real secret ingredient, the fifth and final one: time. Kate Fratar is a certified sommelier and founder and editor of ChasingWine.org, a website dedicated to travel, history, and a study of the world’s varietals. Originally published in the Piedmont Post on August 14, 2019. Casks, contributing approximately 80 to 85 percent of a whisky’s flavor, are being used in new ways to introduce added dimension and complexity as the “fourth” ingredient.

The key is to provide an instant cue for our brains towards something that is already engrained, like the alphabet or the names of relatives, or anything else put into the brain that cannot get out. An ancient memory device, called the Method of Loci, comes from Ancient Greece. To use it, start by imagining a place with which you are familiar. For instance, if you have driven over the bay bridge every day for years imagine the names of the exits as also reading the information you need to memorize. This may be best in the cases where the order of information is crucial. Not every mnemonic device works for everyone. Some people use the acrostic (a poem in which the first letter of each line spells out a word or message) Never Eat Shredded Wheat to remember the points of the compass (North, East, South, West). In addition to remembering the phrase you must also remember to go clockwise and to start at the top. This could be nearly useless for someone with dyslexia. Not all acronyms are created equal either, try to utilize ones that you find funny or that have special meaning to your life. To remember the strings on a guitar E-A-D-G-B-E: Eddie Ate Dynamite Good Bye Eddie may work for those with a macabre sense of humor. Rhymes can help jog memory for those that have a liking for the left-brain; for example: In 1492, Columbus sailed the Ocean Blue. Chunking & Organization is a way to break down larger pieces of information into smaller bits. If you are a sports nut and are trying to remember the digits of pi, try breaking down 3. 14 15 92 65 35 into two digits and associating each with an athlete that wears that number. 3=Babe Ruth, 14=Pete Rose, 15=Vince Carter, 92=Reggie White, 65=Ray Brown (49ers), 35=Kevin Durant. Then by using the letter R, you may find Ruth, Rose, Carter, Reggie, Ray, Durant may help you remember pi. Use what you already know and connect it to what you need to know. Best of luck and happy mnemonic device memorizing. Some people find acrostics as useful mnemonic devices such as My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Nine Pizzas to remember the order of the nine planets (plus Pluto).
